Decisive Campaigns: The Blitzkrieg from Warsaw to Paris is an operational-level World War II wargame developed by VR Designs and published by Matrix Games that focuses on the explosive opening phase of the conflict, where speed, coordination, and planning defined the outcome of entire nations. Rather than centering on individual battles or tactical skirmishes, the game places the player in charge of large formations and long-term objectives, asking them to think like a high command officer overseeing entire campaigns. Its scope spans from the invasion of Poland through the fall of France, capturing the momentum, risks, and fragility behind the concept of Blitzkrieg warfare.

The game’s structure revolves around large hex-based maps that represent vast regions of Europe, with units operating at the regiment, division, and corps level. Every turn requires the player to balance aggressive advances with logistical realities, as supply lines, readiness, and unit cohesion directly affect combat effectiveness. Pushing too hard without securing supply can stall an offensive just as quickly as enemy resistance, while cautious play may allow opponents time to regroup and fortify. This constant tension between speed and sustainability gives the game a strong sense of realism and forces players to think several turns ahead rather than reacting impulsively.

Combat itself is detailed without becoming overly granular. Units are modeled with historically grounded strengths and weaknesses, and success depends heavily on combined arms tactics. Infantry, armor, artillery, and support units must work together to break through defenses or hold critical positions. Terrain plays a major role, with rivers, forests, cities, and road networks shaping movement and engagement outcomes. The result is a system where positioning and preparation matter as much as raw numbers, and where a well-planned encirclement can achieve decisive results without excessive losses.

One of the defining elements of Decisive Campaigns: The Blitzkrieg from Warsaw to Paris is how it integrates strategic decision-making outside of direct combat. Between turns, players face choices that influence production, logistics, command priorities, and political considerations. These decisions add a layer of narrative and consequence to the campaign, making it feel less like a sequence of disconnected battles and more like a living historical operation. Optional “what-if” paths further enhance replayability, allowing campaigns to diverge from historical outcomes and explore alternative possibilities such as extended offensives or altered strategic goals.

The artificial intelligence offers a solid challenge, particularly for players new to operational-level wargames. It is capable of exploiting overextensions, defending key terrain, and applying pressure where weaknesses appear. While experienced players may eventually learn to anticipate its behavior, the AI remains competent enough to keep campaigns engaging and unpredictable. Multiplayer options, including play-by-email, add significant longevity by allowing human opponents to test each other’s strategic foresight and adaptability over extended campaigns.

Visually, the game adopts a clean, utilitarian presentation that emphasizes clarity over spectacle. The interface presents a large amount of information—unit status, supply levels, combat predictions, and strategic overlays—without excessive clutter, though the learning curve can still feel steep for newcomers. The art style is functional rather than immersive, but this restraint ensures that the player’s focus remains on planning and execution rather than visual flair. Once familiar with the interface, managing large-scale operations becomes intuitive and satisfying.

What ultimately sets the game apart is its ability to convey the operational reality of early World War II warfare. Victories feel earned through careful coordination and planning, while failures often stem from overconfidence or neglected logistics rather than bad luck. The game rewards patience, foresight, and a willingness to adapt plans as circumstances change, making each campaign feel like a complex strategic puzzle rather than a scripted historical reenactment.

Decisive Campaigns: The Blitzkrieg from Warsaw to Paris is not a game designed for quick sessions or casual strategy fans, but for players who enjoy deep, thoughtful systems and historically grounded decision-making. It excels at portraying the strengths and vulnerabilities of Blitzkrieg doctrine and offers a compelling sandbox for exploring how early-war campaigns might unfold under different leadership choices. For enthusiasts of operational wargames and World War II history, it stands as a rich, demanding, and highly rewarding strategic experience.

Excellent World War 2 wargame on the operational level. You command an entire army worth of troops on the onset of WW2. There is a campaign which will link the three main scenarios: Case White (Poland '39), Case Yellow (France '40) and Operation Sealion (England '40).

For me this game hits a sweet spot in terms of complexity, scope and depth. You are not mindlessly pushing counters, nor are you completely getting lost in the minutiae of running your command. Your basic counter is generally a regiment, which fits the scope of the game really well. The Order Of Battle is complex enough ranging from your run-of-the-mill infantry regiments up to some very specific named units and even armoured train units.

If you have played any of the Decisive Campaign games you will feel right at home because most of the of the UI and keybinds are similar if not the same. If you have not played any of them and you are a wargamer just give one of them a try  as they are not nearly as difficult to get into as you might expect.

Those who want to try themselves as a general of the Wehrmacht army and conquer Poland, France, and Britain, or save these countries by playing for them, thereby preventing the Second World War - I advise you to play the game: (9 out of 10)

Pros:
✅The game is divided into Campaigns. Battle for Poland, France, and Britain.

✅You can play for several factions: Germany, Britain, Poland, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Slovakia. (Allies on the map are united into one army.)

✅Multiplayer for 6 players, with whom you can go through missions together, each player is given one body. And together with them, attack or defend.

✅The game itself is very convenient for players who want to feel like an army general but don’t bother too much with the systems (simplified supply, system of brigades, divisions, and corps, simple and understandable control of aviation and artillery)

✅Artificial intelligence of decent quality, in a campaign, for example, an attack on Poland, if the corps is threatened with encirclement, the Poles retreat, leaving reserves for cover, blow up bridges, and rush to strengthen themselves in new positions (rivers, cities and important points)

✅In the game, you can create various complications for the campaign, for example, early rainy seasons, which open rivers, thereby complicating the enemy’s progress. Additional troops with the French for the player, or high-quality equipment. There may also be improved troop deployment plans.

✅You can play with NATO icons or regular troops.

✅You can try to complete all campaigns historically. I personally succeeded.

✅Will work on old computers.

✅The game is suitable for both fans of hardcore games of the type (Garry's grisby: war on the east) and those who play Hearts of iron 4.

Minuses:
❌Pretty bad training, immediately scares off players. It scared me off for a few days, and then I decided to go into the campaign myself and figure everything out in ten minutes. It’s much easier to understand the game yourself (although it’s worth reading the manual).

The note:
⚡There is no Ukrainian language - for me, this is not a problem, but I advise some players to take note.

Ach ja. Zur Zeit romantisieren ja hierzulande wieder, zum Glück längst vergangene Tage. Ich nicht. Aber dennoch hat es mich wieder mal in die Decisive Reihe verschlagen. Jeder der drei Teile hat ja seine eigenen Charakter (siehe meine Review zu Barbarossa). Aber "From Warsaw to Paris" ist mir doch der liebste dank dem größten Wiederspielwert. 

Was es ist: 

Ein Strategiespiel auf Operationsbasis. 
Hexfeldstrategie
Turnbased

Was es nicht beinhaltet: 

Großartige Einheitenentwicklung (Erfahrungsanstieg, neue Perks, usw)
Einheitenkauf 
RPG Elemente

Die Kampagne beinhaltet drei Karten. Fall Weiß (Polen). Fall Gelb (Benelux und dann Frankreich) und Seelöwe (Invasion Englands) sowie diese als alleinstehenden Szenarien und im Multiplayer spielbar. 

Wir beginnen wie tausende Male zu vor 1939. Die Truppen stehen an der deutsch/tschechischen/polnischen Grenze in ihren Verfügungsräumen und warten auf unsere genialen Befehle. 

Und dann gehts los. Wie üblich jagen wir unsere Plättchen über die Karte und versuchen mit minimalen eigenen Verlusten Siegpunkte zu erobern. Kennen wir. Was dieses Spiel so besonders macht ist das Kartensystem und zufällige Ereignisse. Es gibt sogeannte politische Punkte, diese dienen als Währung um vor Operationsbeginn verschiedene Karten auszuspielen. Z.B. Wetterbericht oder bessere Aufklärung. Aber auch große Ereignisse wie z.B. amerikanische Freiwillige an der Verteidigung Großbritanniens zu hindern.

Ausserdem wird ab Korpsebene (für Luftwaffensoldaten: Gruppe/Zug/Kompanie/Bataillion/Regiment/Brigade/Division/Korps/Armee/Armeegruppe) die historische Persönlichkeit (die das Korps führt) mit ihren Stärken und Schwächen abgebildet. Diese haben ebenfalls Handkarten um Offensiven, Verteidigung oder Beweglichkeit ihrer unterstellten Gruppenteile zu beeinflussen. Kleinste Spielbare Einheit sind Bataillon und Regiment. 

Die Karten warten mit Events auf. Es gibt EVAC Zonen, die blockiert werden wollen um fliehenden Truppen die Teilnahme an der nächsten Operation zu verwehren. Ihr wisst schon. Das Desast...., äh Wunder von Dünkirchen. Die Niederländer fluten ihre Wälder, die Briten setzten Chemiewaffen ein usw. 

Je nach eigener Leistung spielen sich dann die folgenden Operationen leichter oder schwerer. Und da macht das Spiel einen geilen Job. Anfänglich habe ich mir in Polen wirklich schwer getan und hatte in den folgenden Operationen keine Chance. Also musste ich meine Ungeduld zurücknehmen und mir Zeit nehmen. Kurzum. Ich habe das Spiel so gespielt wie von den Verfassern geplant. Ich habe vor jeder Bewegung und jedem Angriff nachgedacht und bin eine Checkliste durchgegangen. 
Wie ist der Aufklärungslevel des umliegenden Gebietes? Kann es Überraschungen geben? Ist meine Einheit die richtige um anzugreifen? Zusammenhalt. Kampfwert. Moral. Versorgungsgrad. Muss mein Korpschef eine Karte spielen? Wenn ich da hingehe, überdehne ich dann die Versorgung? Lohnt es sich mehr Truppen zu massieren und eine Runde zu warten. Habe ich Artillerie oder Luftwaffe?

Die Luftwaffe funktioniert übrigens wie in echt. Garnicht. Schick an zu sehen, die Herren mit der Zusatzverpflegung, aber recht wirkungslos. 

Der Schwierigkeitsgrad ist übrigens in Teilen anpassbar. 

Also. Für Gary Grigbys Fans ein Muss. Die Komplexität könnte für manche schon als "hardcore Strategie" durchgehen. Also obacht! Es gibt auch nix fürs Auge. Und Fall Gelb ist groß. Eine Runde kann schon bis zu einer Stunde dauern wenn man tatsächlich jede Option prüft.

This is a refreshing old-school hex war-game that doesn't ignore the fact that computers can do book-keeping abstractions better and deeper then Europa type board games, You get all of the minutia of old school games with 100% less rules lawyering.    

So, yeah, you are going to have to work a little harder then a lot of these type games, but not much harder.  The in-game tutorial gets you started, but if you don't go through the manual you're going to screw up.  Maintaining operational and support channels from OKH to divisional units is at first frustrating, and a bit of a learning curve, but you were the one who wanted to invade Poland.  The game makes sure you can get the gas, bullets, and beans where it needs to go, but you're the one who needs to include those logistics in your strategy.    

Happily. once you get it, IT really comes together and you can get on to wrestling with the issue of conquering Western Europe.  The Sealion scenario, and linking Case White, Case Yellow, and Sealion into an extended unified campaign is brilliant.

Un wargame serio (no es sencillo) muy interesante y bien investigado sobre las campañas de la blitzkrieg inicial. Hay otra campaña en Steam (Case Blue) y otra que aún no está en Steam (Barbarrosa) con este mismo motor.

Pros:
- La IA es competente y está bien programada para ponértelo difícil. 
- Históricamente bien detallado y con cosas novedosas (cartas para mandos, por ejemplo).
- La interface es un poco complicada y rara al principio, pero despueés de un par de turnos te haces con ella.
- Modela suministros y HQs muy bien.

Contras:
- La artillería hace poco daño. Da la impresión de que con esto y lo siguiente que comento se intenta igualar un poco la partida (aunque le resta historicismo al juego).
- La aviación está hipersimplificada y hace tan poco daño que casi es mejor no usarla. No puedes atacar aeródromos enemigos, hacer interdicción, etc. Históricamente tuvo un papael mucho más importante del que le atribuye el juego.

Resumen: Un juego muy interesante, que se puede jugar perfectamente contra la IA (algo no muy frecuente en wargames), con una Polonia (es la campaña entera que he jugado) dopada en relación con la historia. Recomendado, especialemente cuando esté de oferta

Sadly can´t recommend, if you like me expect at least some realism and don´t only want to "beat the system":

- very bad tutorial, exhausting usability, ignorance of KISS-principles, manual explains nothing in detail
- Very clunky, user unfriendly interface (no undo command, bad overview of units, ...)
- very unrealistiv combat results (open field, non-entrenced, retreated morale-low infantry without AT-guns not only delays but outright defeats 100+ panzers..., crowded chaotic mega-stacks of morale-low units withstand one and another coordinated attack by combined arms... Surrounded? Hefty losses? No supply lines? HQs and Utility Units in combat? Wayne, we nonetheless hold the line...)
- air force and artillery effect way too low (but many losses because of one (!) enemy AA-Unit...) 
- impossible to deploy real blitzkrieg-tactics: overall too slow unit movement, no strategic (i.e. no combat) movement bonus, too hefty AP-penalty for ZOCs/attacks, attacker penalized by system & too many losses overall (e.g. germany lost about 1% combat strength in the polish campaign, here you try to stay below 10%), no motorized/mechanized/armored overrun system, enemy uses HQ/AA/Artillery-units to block and slow the advance without consequences, because they just retreat in order, attackers have no AP left to attack again... rinse and repeat..., no surrender of surrounded units without attacking them...
- way too random results (roll the dice aaaaaand...)
- confusing display of combat results (and nearly no explanation why things happen the way they do)

Sad, because the game has its strengths:
+ nice, easy supply system
+ very easy air force handling 
+ medium complexity, easy access to game system (between PanzerCorps and WitE)
+ easy organization of corps units
+ rewards for good planing
+ good atmopshere
+ coop play possible
+ interesting historical variants

But all in all: We are not in the 90s anymore... perhaps in a sale.
